**The AI Bubble Is Real—But Not the One Everyone Expects**

### The Circular Money Machine

Major AI companies have built an elaborate web of cross-investments that looks increasingly artificial. Nvidia is pouring up to $100 billion into OpenAI, which in turn guarantees it will buy Nvidia chips for its expansion. Oracle has signed a reported $300 billion computing deal with OpenAI that follows the same pattern. According to The Wall Street Journal and Bloomberg, these circular deals create the appearance of explosive demand while largely moving money between a small group of allied giants.

Wikipedia and multiple analysts have noted that this circular flow is the primary reason serious bubble speculation began in late 2025. When companies effectively invest in each other and then buy each other’s products, stock prices can become detached from genuine end-customer demand.

### Lessons from Dot-com, With Important Differences

Many observers, including Ray Dalio, have drawn direct parallels to the dot-com bubble. Both periods featured sky-high valuations, massive capital expenditure, and breathless predictions about transformative technology. Yet there are meaningful differences. As INSEAD professors Lin Shen, Lily Fang, and Ben Charoenwong point out, today’s leading AI beneficiaries—Microsoft, Alphabet, Nvidia—are already highly profitable cash-flow machines, unlike many dot-com era companies that were burning cash on marketing with no clear path to profit.

The infrastructure being built (data centers, chips, power) is also far more redeployable than the marketing spend and bespoke websites of the late 1990s. Federal Reserve Chair Powell has publicly stated that AI represents a genuine source of economic growth in a way the dot-com bubble never did before it burst.

### Where the Real Bubble May Be Hiding

The consensus emerging from Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan, and Fidelity analysts is that the listed market may not be in a classic bubble—yet—but the pre-IPO startup ecosystem almost certainly is. Venture capitalists continue to pour money into cash-burning AI companies with no clear route to profitability. When that capital dries up, many of those firms will disappear, exactly as happened to countless VC-backed dot-com companies after 2000.

Meanwhile, the next phase of AI—humanoid robotics and embodied intelligence—is only beginning to appear in valuations. Goldman Sachs estimates the global market for humanoid robots could reach $38 billion by 2035, suggesting the current frenzy may be focused on the wrong part of the technology stack.

**What this means:** We are not looking at a simple “pop or not” scenario. The underlying technology is real and will likely transform the economy, but the current concentration of capital, circular deal-making, and sky-high expectations have created classic bubble conditions in parts of the market. The correction, when it comes, will probably hurt early-stage startups and speculative investors far more than the major public AI infrastructure companies. The question is not whether there will be disappointment—there always is after periods of extreme hype—but how widely and how deeply the damage will spread when the cooling-off inevitably arrives.
